blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables language-model agents to improve
through multi-turn interaction with verifiable environments, but long horizons
and sparse outcome rewards make successful behavior difficult to discover and
reinforce ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) .
Textual skills can ease this challenge by compressing trajectories or feedback
into reusable procedural guidance for subsequent decisions ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) .
Existing approaches extract, refine, and retrieve such guidance using external
memory or teacher models ( Nottingham et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) .
SkillRL, for example, uses a stronger teacher to build an evolving SkillBank,
turning sparse trajectory-level feedback into guidance for subsequent
exploration ( Xia et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
To address these challenges, we propose SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training
scaffold for agentic RL, summarized in Figure 1 .
Its core idea is to replace candidate-specific environment evaluation with
outcome-aware likelihood comparisons on existing training trajectories.
A shared policy serves as both an Executor , which collects skill-free
Scout trajectories, and a Generator , which produces candidate skills
from outcome-labeled Scout evidence.
For each candidate, SkillScaffold rescores fixed Scout evidence under candidate-skill
and no-skill contexts to obtain a policy-relative utility estimate.
This proxy favors increased likelihood of successful behavior and reduced
likelihood of observed failures, according to the available outcome evidence.
The highest-utility candidate guides fresh Executor rollouts only when its
estimated utility is positive; otherwise, execution remains skill-free.
Environment rewards supervise the Executor, while skill utility supervises
the Generator through role-specific GRPO objectives, enabling the Generator
to adapt its guidance to the evolving Executor.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training scaffold for skill credit
assignment in agentic RL. Rather than assuming generated skills are helpful or
evaluating every candidate through additional environment interaction, SkillScaffold reuses outcome-verified trajectories to estimate policy-relative
utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons. This signal supports
candidate ranking, abstention, and Generator learning, while environment
outcomes continue to supervise the Executor. Across diverse short- and
long-horizon benchmarks, SkillScaffold improves over strong agentic-RL and
skill-based RL baselines under fully skill-free inference. Overall, SkillScaffold selectively uses skills to improve training-time exploration, absorbs their
guidance into the policy, and removes the skill pathway at deployment.

Focus on the metal fork to examine its properties. 2. Pick up the metal fork to place it in the inventory. 3. Check for the presence of a power source and light bulb in the environment. 4. Connect the metal fork to the power source and light bulb to form a circuit. 5. Observe if the light bulb illuminates to determine conductivity. 6. If the light bulb lights up, place the metal fork in the destination specified by the current task. ## Decision rules If the light bulb does not illuminate, check the connections and ensure the circuit is complete. If the power source or light bulb is not available, do not proceed with the test. If the connection command is rejected, verify the presence of the required objects before retrying. ## Verification and recovery Confirm that the light bulb lights up as a clear signal of conductivity.
